title: Given n nodes labeled 0 to n minus 1 and a list of undirected edges, return the number of connected components in the graph.
shortTitle: Number of Connected Components: Union-Find or DFS
keyPoints: Start with n singleton components and union each edge's endpoints, decrementing on each merge
Path compression and union by rank give near-constant amortized time per operation
A DFS/BFS sweep counts how many traversals are needed to visit all nodes, giving the same answer
Union-Find is ideal for incremental edge additions and repeated connectivity queries
DFS is simpler for a static graph where no edges are added after construction
Time is effectively O(V + E) for Union-Find with optimizations; space is O(V) for the parent and rank arrays

s1_definition.oneliner: Start with n components and union each edge's endpoints, decrementing the count on each merge; the remaining count is the number of connected components.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Connected components** are groups of mutually reachable nodes in an undirected graph.
- **Union-Find** starts with n singletons, merges endpoints of each edge, and decrements the count on each successful merge.
- **Path compression** flattens the tree toward the root during find, keeping operations fast.
- **Union by rank** attaches the shallower tree under the deeper one, preventing degenerate chains.
- **DFS alternative** counts how many traversals are needed to visit all nodes.
- **Time** is O(V + E * alpha(V)) which is effectively linear; **space** is O(V).
s1_definition.analogy: Think of counting separate clusters of linked accounts at the National Bank of India. Every account starts as its own cluster. Each link you discover merges two clusters into one if they were separate, reducing the count by one. When all links are processed, the number of clusters left is the answer.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Number of Connected Components counts the groups of mutually reachable nodes. Union-Find starts with each of the n nodes as its own component, processes each edge by finding the roots of its endpoints, and merges them when they differ, decrementing the count. Path compression and union by rank keep the operations near-constant, making the whole algorithm effectively linear.

The DFS alternative builds an adjacency list and counts how many traversals are needed to visit all nodes. Each DFS invocation explores one complete component. For a static graph, DFS is simpler to implement. For dynamic edges or repeated connectivity queries, Union-Find is the clear winner because it handles additions incrementally.

The common pitfall is forgetting path compression, which degrades find to O(n). Another is not checking whether two nodes are already in the same component before decrementing the count, though the root comparison naturally handles this.

At the National Bank of India, linked accounts formed fraud clusters. The fraud team needed the number of distinct clusters, and because links arrived incrementally, Union-Find merged clusters in near-constant time and always had the current count available.

Remember one sentence: start with n components, union each edge, decrement on merge, and the remainder is the component count.
